死间.note: Literally “dead agent”; one of the five kinds of spy in Sun Tzu’s Art of War, and Juntong’s term for agents planted to burrow into the Communist base areas.

海底.note: Juntong jargon (literally “sea bottom”) for the secret personal dossier each agent memorized—names, addresses, contacts, cipher, and oath—left on file at the training class.

汉中特训班.note: Juntong’s special training class near Hanzhong, run under the cover name “Tianshui Field Headquarters Guerrilla Cadre Training Class”; called the “Hanzhong class” (汉训班) for short.

汉训班.note: Short form of the Hanzhong training class.

戴案.note: The Border Security’s name for the Hanzhong-class case, after Dai Li, whose Juntong system ran the agents.

西北特别侦察站.note: Juntong’s Xi’an-based station (西北特侦站 for short) directing the penetration of the Northwest base areas; headed by Cheng Muyi.

吴南山.note: The Qingyang schoolteacher who graduated the Hanzhong class, came forward to the Communists, and became the Border Security’s long-hidden field operative in Longdong; the case began with him.

程慕颐.note: Chief of Juntong’s Northwest Special Reconnaissance Station and deputy director of the Hanzhong class (cover name Cheng Yi); fled to Taiwan.

程益.note: Cover name of Cheng Muyi as director of the Hanzhong class.

祁三益.note: Hanzhong-class demolition instructor sent to Yan’an as group liaison; turned by the Border Security and central to cracking the case.

李春茂.note: Hanzhong-class liaison (aliases Li Changsheng, Li Jun); turned and taken into the Border Security.

赵秀.note: Chief liaison for the Northwest Station’s Yan’an group; briefly turned, later fled back to Xi’an.

王星文.note: Hanzhong agent (alias Wang Jiwu) at the Lu Xun Academy of Arts; turned by the Border Security.

胡士渊.note: Leader of the independent cell (aliases Hu Siyuan, Hu Yaonan, Hu Youlian) planted in the Military Commission’s Second Bureau.

布鲁.note: Chen Bo (陈泉), the Border Security’s security-work chief, the “Red Sherlock Holmes”; led the cracking of the case.

马文瑞.note: 1912–2004. Longdong prefectural party secretary who took Wu Nanshan in; himself once wrongly arrested in the northern-Shaanxi purge. Later a vice-chairman of the CPPCC National Committee.

李甫山.note: Longdong security-section chief who ran Wu Nanshan; later head of the Border Security office in Yan’an.

赵苍壁.note: 1916–1993. Border Security plainclothes-squad head sent to Longdong; later Minister of Public Security.

王珺.note: Social Affairs Department officer of the “Old Third Class” who traced the Second Bureau cell; later deputy minister of State Security.

周兴.note: Head of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Security Office and deputy commander of the Yan’an garrison.

戴笠.note: 1897–1946. Head of Juntong, the Nationalists’ military secret service.

欧阳毅.note: 1910–2005. Head of the General Political Department’s Anti-Traitor Department, which handled the army-system agents; later a PLA lieutenant general.

钱益民.note: Investigation expert of the General Political Department’s Anti-Traitor Department, one of Yan’an’s “three great investigation experts.”

ch08.note: “Expendable agents” renders 死间 (sijian), literally “dead agents”—one of the five kinds of spy in Sun Tzu’s Art of War, the doomed agent fed false information and sent knowing he is likely to be caught and killed. Juntong used the term for the men it planted to burrow into the Communist base areas, as Sun Tzu’s spy-types are glossed earlier in the book.

The haidi (海底, literally “sea bottom”) was Juntong jargon for the secret personal dossier each agent compiled and memorized: his real and cover names, his permanent and mailing addresses, the cover names of his contacts, the cipher for their correspondence, and his oath. The original stayed on file at the training class, and all later clandestine contact was keyed to it.

The Renaissance Society (复兴社) was an outer organ of the Nationalist “Blue Shirts,” the network of Chiang Kai-shek loyalists built in the early 1930s around the inner Vigorous Action Society (力行社), noted earlier in the book. Its members served as Nationalist party and security cadres.

Ren Zhuoxuan (任卓宣, 1896–1990), pen name Ye Qing, was an early Communist—once head of the Party’s Paris branch—who, after his arrest, defected and became the Nationalists’ foremost anti-Communist theorist and a propaganda official. Kang Sheng cites his career as the model of a turncoat put to use. (Corroborated.)

The chapter gives several figures because they count different things from different sources. The 32 agents of the core Yan’an “Dai case” (1 who came forward, 20 found by investigation, 11 named by others) are the single case cracked in 1942; a later recollection puts the Yan’an arrests at forty-odd and the whole Yan’an-period haul at 55; the 631 trained over nine sessions is the Gansu investigators’ 1955 count for the entire class, close to Cheng Muyi’s own captured report of 670, against 320 known earlier and 160 newly found. The book does not reconcile the tallies.

The People’s Liberation Army’s assault on Yijiangshan (一江山), a small island off the Zhejiang coast held by the Nationalists, in January 1955 was China’s first combined army-navy-air amphibious landing; the captured documents included Cheng Muyi’s report. (Corroborated.)
The Bureau of Confidential Investigation (保密局, Baomiju) was the postwar successor to Juntong, formed in 1946 under the Defense Ministry; that renaming is why the wartime Juntong is meant here.

Baigongguan (白公馆, the “White Mansion”), a villa at Geleshan outside Chongqing, served Juntong as a prison and as part of its Chongqing training apparatus; it belonged to the SACO complex noted in Chapter 7, where many captured Communists were held and killed.
